#331. Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert

Lawsuit: Over 99% of school system’s AI gun alerts were false positives.

In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.

Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.

The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.

According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.

At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit said.

“No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit said. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”

Only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.

“Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly said. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”

The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.

Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.

The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.

Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—said that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”

The complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.

“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt said. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”

All the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.

Car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, said his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”

Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.

“The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield said. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”

The teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a canceled alert.

In a later investigation, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was canceled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.

The OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct biannual trainings moving forward.

They also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG said.

Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”

Another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.

These recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of whom remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report said, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.

“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.

The teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.

BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.

Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.

“What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell said. “We understand why they want answers.”

Mitchell said that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.

“In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and canceled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell said. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a canceled alert must stay canceled.”

Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The New York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”

“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang said.

As a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she said.

“I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield said. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”

Kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”

As AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release said. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#330. 2023 March Madness: Will UConn or San Diego State triumph in the national championship game that 'means everything?'

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He said going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

“We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher said. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

“They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he said.

UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

#329. Streaming GTA 6? Turn this setting on so you dont get copyright strikes.

Grand Theft Auto VI has quite a stacked soundtrack.

Cardi B, Travis Scott, Dua Lipa, Justice, Lana Del Rey — these are just some of the artists whose music can be heard on dozens of in-game radio stations.

GTA 6's plethora of licensed music has led to some viral moments, like the clip of streamer caseoh rocking out to Ariana Grande in real life while chilling out in a car in the game.

However, as fun as those moments can be, there is a danger to being a livestreamer while playing licensed, copyrighted music during a stream. While Rockstar Games gives permission to online creators to stream and create videos with their own music created for the game, that doesn't extend to licensed music from record labels and artists. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

An in-game licensed song playing on your YouTube or Twitch channel can get your content taken down. Creators can also receive copyright strikes, which can result in demonetization or in some cases complete removal of their account.

Thankfully, Rockstar Games has kept streamers and content creators in mind and gave them an easy way to shut off licensed music. Here's how to do it.

Simply pause the game by pressing the option or menu button on your controller.

Next, scroll down to the Settings option.

In the Settings menu, head to the very last tab labeled Audio.

Finally, scroll down to Mute Licensed Music and toggle this option on.

This option will mute all the licensed music in the game and ensure your streams and videos don't get taken down.

There are some things to note. Rockstar Games does not provide any royalty-free replacement music. If a licensed song is playing on the radio in-game, users won't hear anything until a radio show host or original song comes on. With that said, original music created for the game will continue to play. In addition, captions for licensed music will still appear on screen even though the music won't be audible.

You can always roll the dice and hope a song played on the radio in GTA 6 doesn't take down your stream or clip. But, this Mute Licensed Music option will help you avoid any potential issues.

#328. Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."

25-year-old accused of stalking employees at coffee shop and in an “aggressive” car pursuit.

A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly said he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”

Prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully in the summer of 2026 after being recruited by someone over Telegram. Prosecutors said the party gave D’iu a clandestine assignment to target employees of a large technology and defense company. D’iu received instructions, equipment, and financial support along with information that his work was on behalf of “the motherland.” His instructions were to collect information about the company because it was supplying weapons for use against Russian forces in Ukraine.

Prosecutors said D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City in June. He then crossed the border into the US and was instructed to buy laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software. Besides instructions to monitor company employees at the coffee shop, D’iu’s orders also included positioning his laptop at certain locations near the company so it could be remotely accessed in an attempt to collect information from company employees nearby.

D’iu allegedly obtained fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity as he conducted his activities. The documents included a falsified California ID card, an altered US passport, and a Social Security card bearing the assumed name of “Hugo Landry Johns.” The passport was allegedly an authentic US passport that originally had been issued to someone elsewhere in the country. It was modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.

D’iu was arrested on October 30 and remains in custody. He is charged with one count of Conspiracy to Act as an Agent of a Foreign Government, one count of Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, and one count of Interstate Stalking. If convicted for Acting as an Agent of a Foreign Government Without Notice to the Attorney General, he faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release. He faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison, a fine of $250,000, and three years of supervised release for each conviction on the other two charges.

D’iu had his initial appearance in federal court on November 2. He is next scheduled to appear in federal court on November 24.

#325. Uber is testing rides for kids as young as 10

Getting kids where they need to go is a job in itself. Between school, extracurriculars, and appointments, families often piece together rides with help from relatives and other parents.

Uber is testing whether it can take on some of that driving.

The company's new pilot, Uber Kids, lets parents and guardians book rides for children ages 10 to 12 to take on their own. The service is available to select families in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin, starting Nov. 19. This comes after some rumors: Bloomberg first reported in August that Uber was developing the option.

Here's what parents should know before booking, from how to set up a ride to how to follow it in real time.

To book a ride, a parent or guardian first adds their child to the Family hub in the Uber app. Then they select the child as the rider. If the pilot is available to their family, Uber Kids will appear as a ride option, and the app will guide them through adding pickup and drop-off details.

Kids don't need their own Uber account or app. They can get updates about the trip by text at the number listed on their profile. Parents can request rides from 5 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily, as long as a driver is available.

Each ride goes straight to one destination. A parent or the adult handling pickup can ride along, and kids ages 10 to 17 can join with their guardian’s permission, as long as the child the ride was booked for is in the car. And, if no Uber Kids driver is available, a child ages 10 to 12 needs an adult to ride with them in a regular Uber.

A parent or another adult selected in the app must be at pickup to give the driver the PIN that starts the ride. If someone else needs to handle pickup or drop-off after booking, the guardian contacts the driver and sends the new adult the trip details and tracking link. Only the guardian can change the destination in the app.

Once the car is moving, the guardian can track it on a map, contact the driver, or tap "Watch" to see live video from the driver's phone. The driver gets a notification when the feed starts, and only the guardian and safety agents can watch it. Uber can flag an unexpected stop or route change so a safety agent can check in. Kids can also call their guardian or the support number in their trip texts. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

At drop-off, the driver confirms the child reached the entrance or met the adult assigned to greet them. If that person hasn't arrived, the driver tries to reach them or the guardian, then calls Uber's safety line if nobody answers.

The app also makes a separate audio and video recording. Neither the guardian nor the driver can access it. Uber says it receives the encrypted recording only if someone reports a safety incident. Otherwise, it’s deleted after 14 days.

Uber says it invites experienced, highly rated drivers who have passed a background check. Drivers have to complete a training module on how Uber Kids trips work and turn on audio and video recording in the Driver app. Uber's driver guide explains how drivers should handle pickup and drop-off.

It's interesting that Uber is expanding to younger riders as it faces thousands of lawsuits from passengers who say they were sexually assaulted by drivers.

As of Nov. 2, 4,548 cases were pending in the coordinated federal litigation, according to the U.S. Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation. In February, a federal jury in Arizona found Uber liable and awarded $8.5 million to a woman who said a driver raped her when she was 19. And in April, a North Carolina jury awarded $5,000 in a related case after finding that a driver committed battery. (Uber settled another federal case in October before it went to trial.)

Uber has been giving teens a way to get around on their own since 2023. Kids ages 13 to 17 can request rides through an account linked to a parent's account, and Lyft offers a similar service in select areas called "Lyft Teen." When a child in the Uber Kids pilot turns 13, they can set up a teen account and request their own ride (or their parents can still do it for them).

Families with younger kids already have options like HopSkipDrive, which takes riders as young as 6. The company says its drivers need at least five years of caregiving experience and must pass a fingerprint-based background check. There's no saying whether Uber utilizes similar investigations.

For plenty of families, getting to practice or a lesson still means a parent does the driving. In a 2025 survey by AP-NORC and HopSkipDrive, 75 percent of parents whose kids participated in extracurriculars said they drove their kids themselves. When asked about the school commute, 28 percent of K–12 parents said they considered a hired ride, like a taxi, Uber, or Lyft, at least somewhat safe for their child.

This pilot will ultimately test whether features like a PIN at pickup and live video during the ride make parents comfortable enough to book one.

#324. Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?

Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

#323. MAHA PAC spent more on steak, luxury club than candidates, report shows

Expert called MAHA’s spending “pretty unusual” for a PAC.

In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA’s own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group’s priority was ever winning elections in the first place.

The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.

The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.

According to Stat’s findings, of the $10.5 million the MAHA PAC spent on the midterms, less than a tenth—roughly $1 million—went to messaging on political candidates, which are expenses called “independent expenditures.”

Andrew Mayersohn, a committees researcher at OpenSecrets, called the spending “pretty unusual,” explaining that “Major super PACs spend most of their money on independent expenditures.”

In some cases, the scant political spending was dwarfed by spending on luxuries. For instance, in a key House race in Northern California, MAHA supported Kevin Kiley over his political rival, pediatrician Richard Pan. Despite calling the race “the most direct ideological confrontation” between MAHA and its opposition “anywhere on the 2026 ballot,” the PAC only spent $49,900 to back Kiley. That’s a little less than the $50,100 it spent at Mastro’s Steakhouse, an upscale restaurant that offers $110 porterhouse steaks in Washington, DC. Further, it’s less than a third of the $155,900 the PAC spent at Ned’s Club, a luxury club near the White House that has become a popular gathering spot among Trump officials.

Kiley lost the election to Pan by double digits.

Of the roughly $1 million spent on political candidates, most of it—over $700,000—went to defeating Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.). Many other MAHA-endorsed candidates received $50,000 or less. Some got less than $2,000.

Outside of steaks and a private club, the MAHA PAC spent $500,000 on a media company, Merit Street Media, run by Phil McGraw, who hosted a MAHA special featuring Dr. Phil. MAHA leaders used PAC money to cover meals, payroll, and credit card bills. The PAC paid $275,000 to a security firm, Gavin de Becker & Associates, which is led by an ally of anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., MAHA’s top leader. Tens of thousands more went to LLCs that have little to no online information.

On the other hand, prominent online MAHA influencers also pocketed tens of thousands from the PAC, as did writers for The MAHA Report, a Substack that promotes Kennedy and MAHA interests. In the days after the midterms, as members of the movement were coming to grips with the election losses, The MAHA Report chose to publish a lengthy article defending convicted rapist Russel Brand, a Kennedy ally who became a MAHA fixture.

The biggest chunk of the MAHA PAC’s spending—more than $3 million—went to the nonprofit MAHA Action, which is also run by Lyons. It’s unclear how all that money was spent.

#322. Uber Kids will let parents book trips for their children aged 10 to 12 years old

It's a limited pilot program available in just three locations for now.

Uber is giving parents and guardians the option to get their kids a special ride they can track and monitor, at least in a few specific locations. The ride-hailing company has started testing a new service called Uber Kids meant for children aged 10 to 12 years old. According to TechCrunch, it rolled out quietly in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee and Madison, Wisconsin over the past weeks.

The company already has Uber for Teens, but that program lets teenagers aged 13 to 17 make bookings from their own accounts, as long as they're part of a Family profile with a parent or guardian. For Uber Kids, only parents and guardians can order a ride for their children, and they must be present at pickup. Like on rides taken by teens, they'll also be able to access live video feed from inside the car to check in on their child in real time. Guardians themselves can come on the trip, along with additional minors, as long as they have their own parents' or guardians' permission. However, multi-stop rides aren't allowed on Uber Kids, and all trips booked under the program must be to a single destination.

Uber isn't sending Kids ride requests to all drivers on its network. The company is only inviting highly rated drivers to participate in the program, and those interested will have to complete a short course to be able to get in. They will also be required to enable audio and video recordings on their app, as well as to switch on camera and microphone access so that guardians can watch their kids on the ride. Uber says drivers will be notified once Live Video starts and that only the kids' guardians and safety agents will be able to access the realt-time feed.

Since Kids rides come with all these requirements, Uber will pay drivers $7 more compared to a standard UberX trip. Drivers will also get an additional $20 for the first Kids trip they complete. As TechCrunch notes, though, this is just a limited pilot program, and it's not clear if the company has plans to expand it to more locations in the future.

#321. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#318. Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up

Amazon now uses its shopping platform for political purposes.

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.

When I log in to Amazon today, I’m met with a vertical banner that reads: “ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order” with a button that says “Act now.”

I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged in to Amazon.

Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:

Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is new is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

The messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any company with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

It also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the new pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its users.

Given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports.

Finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

The Delivery Protection Act is currently stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

#317. Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?

From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.

The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

#316. Teenage swimmer breaks two world records in four days

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh said, per Reuters.

“It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.

#315. The Trump administration has replaced its cybersecurity chief

Sean Cairncross was ousted following several high-profile tech outages.

Sean Cairncross is no longer the US National Cyber Director. The Trump administration has fired him, following several tech outages in the country, according to Reuters. If you'll recall, Microsoft's services recently went down and remained offline for almost a full day, which had affected businesses, hospitals and even governments around the world. The Federal Aviation Administration had also ordered a nationwide ground stop that had disrupted more than 18,000 flights inside, to and from the US.

It's not quite clear why the White House removed Cairncross in relation to those incidents, but the government has been getting flak over its response to cybersecurity threats, including those posed by advanced AI agents and tools. Cairncoss oversaw the administration's cybersecurity strategy, as well as the implementation of related policies across the federal government. According to Axios, however, Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, wanted him out because he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job." The president, "fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," Reuters' source said.

In a statement, Cairncross said he was proud of what he had done "to strengthen America's cyber security, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in super intelligence."

Kirsten A. Davies, the Department of Defense's chief information officer, will now serve as the new US National Cyber Director. Davies had held cybersecurity-related posts in the private sector before, including in companies like Hewlett-Packard and Siemens. The administration reportedly believes she has the experience and the credentials needed to be able to excel in the position.
