#313. Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

TP-Link’s struggle illustrates how Trump admin wields control over device makers.

TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn’t been able to obtain an exemption.

The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

TP-Link’s struggle is not much of a surprise, given its history as a Chinese company and the Trump administration’s focus on reducing reliance on Chinese and other foreign technology. While TP-Link faces political challenges related to the Trump administration’s push for on-shoring, its problems go deeper: It must convince the government its routers aren’t vulnerable to foreign hacking campaigns and that its routers are not Chinese-controlled technology, as suggested at a congressional committee hearing last year.

TP-Link was founded in 1996 in China but has since split into two companies, with one in the US. The US-based TP-Link established California as its global headquarters in October 2024, months after completing a “formal organizational separation” from the TP-Link entity in China.

“TP-Link has split from and no longer has any affiliation with TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd., which serves the mainland Chinese market. Despite having similar names, these companies have entirely different ownership, management, and operations,” TP-Link says.

TP-Link opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Archer 8 Ultra, in September, though not in the US. It’s expected to ship this month and costs £899.99 in the UK, or about $1,178. Since it’s priced like a luxury device, its unavailability in the US won’t make a difference to most consumers. But it’s unknown how long it will take TP-Link to gain permission to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, or whether it will receive permission at all.

TP-Link has pledged to assemble all new routers in the US, but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task. The government reviews of router makers’ requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy. From the outside, it is unclear whether the Trump administration applies consistent security criteria to all companies or whether it grants waivers to favored companies without regard to the actual security of their products.

Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews. SpaceX’s Starlink division obtained a waiver for its routers, while Amazon received a waiver covering routers for its Leo satellite broadband service and the devices sold by its Eero subsidiary. There have been 26 waivers issued so far, covering products made by firms such as Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax, and Vantiva.

Some US lawmakers seem to think the FCC process covers too many products. House Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) and Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) proposed legislation in September that would limit the FCC’s authority to place entire categories of equipment on the list of banned products, as it did with routers.

The Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require the FCC to report to Congress a week before adding any new technology or service to what’s known as the Covered List and require new additions to include only technologies or services produced or provided by an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. That means China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran.

“The current process for identifying and barring malicious foreign technology has worked in many cases, but lacks the transparency, consistency, and clarity needed to meet our long-term national security needs as technology rapidly advances,” Pallone and Guthrie said in a joint statement.

The Pentagon declined Ars’ request for comment on TP-Link’s request for an exemption. The FCC and Department of Homeland Security did not provide any comment.

The US ban on all foreign routers was part of a dramatic expansion of the Covered List, which is managed by the FCC in consultation with the Commerce Department and federal agencies with national security expertise. The Covered List was created by a 2020 law and received its first additions in March 2021. It applies to products that “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”

For the first few years of the Covered List’s existence, only specific companies were added. This included Chinese device-makers Huawei and ZTE, several video surveillance product makers, the Russian security company Kaspersky Lab, and several Chinese telecom companies. Under the Trump administration, new additions to the list include entire product categories, regardless of whether a particular vendor has been identified as a risk. In addition to routers, the Covered List currently includes foreign drones, robotic devices, and power inverters.

A former government official told Ars that the Covered List isn’t as useful as it should be.

“The government needs to be able to quickly identify national security risks and, to the extent that they can, you’ve got to give the public and industry guidance on what to do in order to avoid that risk,” said Betsy McIntyre, a lawyer and consultant who previously worked for the FCC on telecom mergers and at the Department of Justice on national security reviews of foreign investment in telecom. “That’s why I have always loved the Covered List. It’s this great tool. It’s simple. It has so much potential to guide procurement decisions for small businesses, large businesses. It can even help when moms are going to Best Buy and figuring out what kinds of equipment they should be buying.”

McIntyre doesn’t like the approach of adding entire categories of products to the list, rather than specific products from individual companies.

“The ideal Covered List would be, as soon as there’s a problem, it would be updated,” she said. “They’d name a company, and then people know: ‘don’t buy this’ or ‘this kind of equipment poses a national security risk.’ It’s a little bit muddled now.”

Although the FCC maintains the Covered List, McIntyre said the FCC’s role was set up at the beginning to be “very ministerial.” The FCC would add companies or products to the list based on determinations by national security agencies, with the FCC having no discretion once it received a determination.

McIntyre noted that she was not privy to any of the discussions that led to the broad inclusion of routers this year. It’s not necessarily clear to the public why any particular item is added to the list or why any company receives an exemption, because “the national security decision-making process can be a black box,” she said.

TP-Link routers formed the bulk of a botnet controlled by Chinese threat actors, Microsoft said in 2024. But TP-Link is far from the only router maker whose products have vulnerabilities. Routers made by US companies Cisco and Netgear were part of a botnet of devices hijacked by Chinese state-sponsored attackers in 2023, the Justice Department said after taking action to remove the malware.

Security expert Bruce Schneier said there’s no reason to think TP-Link routers are less secure than those of its competitors. “They’re all awful. They’re all equally awful,” he told Ars.

Computers and smartphones generally have strong security because companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft “have massive security teams designing these things to be good in the first place and writing patches when flaws are found,” Schneier said.

With routers, webcams, smart refrigerators, wireless drones, and Internet of Things devices in general, “there’s no one on staff to deal with a security vulnerability… These are just less secure devices because the economics of them doesn’t reward security. The way you patch a lot of your home routers is you throw it away and buy a new one. That’s the patch mechanism.”

When asked about TP-Link facing more scrutiny because of its history as a Chinese company, Schneier said that router makers are “all Chinese companies… I don’t care what [name] you stick on the box. They’re all made in China.”

TP-Link is pledging to assemble routers in the US, though it would still use parts from overseas. Schneier said that “these are distinctions that don’t matter that much.”

TP-Link says the devices it sells in the US are made in Vietnam. But an April 2025 Bloomberg article said, “TP-Link confirmed that, aside from components bought in Vietnam that account for 0.5 percent of the total value of inputs to the plant there, all other components are imported from China.”

TP-Link declined an interview request from Ars this month. “Aside from what’s already out there, the company doesn’t have any new updates to share right now,” a TP-Link spokesperson told us.

TP-Link could sue the government, but litigation can drag out for years. Drone makers have been subject to the same kind of FCC import ban since December 2025, and Chinese drone maker DJI sued the FCC in February. FCC and Justice Department lawyers urged the court to dismiss the lawsuit as “premature,” because the FCC hasn’t made a final decision on a petition that DJI filed with the FCC. The US government’s latest motion to dismiss the lawsuit is still pending with the Ninth Circuit appeals court, and the FCC hasn’t ruled on the petition for reconsideration that DJI filed in January.

Several developments over the past two years make it unsurprising that TP-Link hasn’t obtained a waiver. US officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban due to national security risks during the final months of the Biden administration. The government separately probed TP-Link last year in an antitrust investigation reportedly focused on whether it sold goods below cost to gain a dominant share of the US router market.

The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party held a March 2025 hearing on deterring China’s hacking attacks and improving what the committee called “America’s lackluster cyber defenses.” Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity for the National Security Agency, said in testimony that China is “undercutting our market to deliver Chinese-controlled technologies into our homes” and named TP-Link as the prime example.

“TP-Link, the world’s largest manufacturer of commercial Wi-Fi and home routers, has grown to at least 60 percent of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and SoHo [Small Office and Home Office] routers compared with about 10 percent of the market at the start of 2019,” he said. “How have they achieved this miraculous growth? They appear to be selling at price points below profitability to drive out the western competition… TP-Link routers were among the various brands exploited by Chinese state-sponsored hackers in the massive Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon attacks… We cannot have the software for these prolific devices be written, updated, and controlled by a Chinese company. By law, such a company is subject to the direction of the PRC [People’s Republic of China] Intelligence apparatus. This is a threat we cannot ignore.”

TP-Link said in a March 2025 response to Joyce’s comments that its “products are not ‘Chinese-controlled technology,’” that “all of TP-Link’s R&D operations globally are owned and controlled by TP-Link’s US headquarters,” and that “no government—including the PRC—has access to and control over the design and production of TP-Link routers.”

In 2023, the year before Biden administration officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban, TP-Link boasted of being “the world’s No. 1 Wi-Fi product provider for 12 years running” based on analyst firm IDC’s tracking of worldwide shipments. More recently, TP-Link has argued that estimates of its dominance are wildly inflated, at least in the US.

TP-Link’s response to Joyce said it held “a 36.6 percent unit share and a 31 percent dollar share of the US consumer router market during 2024.” The company says in a fact sheet that when routers provided to users by Internet service providers are taken into account, “TP-Link’s market share of residential Wi-Fi router sales in North America in 2024 was under 10 percent.”

Florida and three other states with Republican attorneys general sued TP-Link last month, alleging that it lied to consumers about connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers. A group of 21 Republican state AGs also sent a letter to the FCC, urging it to address alleged violations of state laws in its review of TP-Link’s waiver request. TP-Link told the FCC that the “heightened standard” demanded by state attorneys general “would be unattainable to TP-Link or any other router manufacturer in the world.”

Last month, the FCC warned TP-Link that several of its existing routers exceeded power limits. These include devices already being used by US consumers, such as the Archer BE670 tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router.

“Based on our evaluation of the purchased samples, we have tentatively determined that TP-Link included false or incorrect information in its applications for these equipment authorizations; and these devices do not operate consistently with the parameters power levels [sic] submitted in the certification applications,” the FCC told TP-Link.

TP-Link told Bloomberg that any routers exceeding power limits are an aberration and that the four products identified by the FCC account for less than one-third of 1 percent of the company’s total US unit sales this year. Nonetheless, the power-limit investigation related to TP-Link’s existing routers may be a bad sign for its chances of getting a waiver to import and sell Wi-Fi 8 routers.

TP-Link told reporter Dong Ngo that the FCC tests were “routine spot checks.” But FCC officials may have examined existing TP-Link devices because of the pending request for a waiver from the Covered List.

“Any time a company has significant requests before the agency, it’s not unusual if the agency is making sure that the company is behaving in a manner the way they expect it to, complying with the rules,” said Jeremy Marcus, a lawyer who spent over 20 years in government in multiple roles, including deputy chief of the FCC Enforcement Bureau.

Marcus declined to discuss TP-Link specifically. He noted that the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology has ongoing market surveillance programs. But when a company has larger issues pending at the FCC, the Office of Engineering and Technology may “do their own due diligence to make sure that existing equipment is performing the way it’s authorized to,” he said.

Although TP-Link has since gone a bit quiet and declined an interview request from Ars, a company official previously spoke to other publications about the FCC waiver process. TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag last month that “there isn’t a lot of clarity” in the government’s demands for US-built technology. Many components used in routers are only available from foreign countries, he said.

“There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” he said. “Or what about, we buy our chipsets for these products from Qualcomm and Broadcom. Is that a US product?”

Kovsky’s background is in corporate marketing and communications, and he started at TP-Link a year ago in a contracting role as a senior communications strategist and consultant. He was hired as the corporate affairs officer in June and has been the main public speaker on the company’s attempts to get a Covered List waiver.

Kovsky expressed some optimism last month. “We have no problem with the FCC, and are really looking forward to pursuing this, and really setting the standard for transparency, and showing that we have the ability to perform and meet all of these criteria with flying colors,” Kovsky told PCMag. “I don’t know if every manufacturer could say the same thing.”

Kovsky spoke to The Verge around the same time, defending the company’s security. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever,” he said. “We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category, to my knowledge.”

Kovsky also downplayed TP-Link’s router market share in the US. “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three,” he said. “It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.”

Kovsky pleaded with government officials for a quick approval in a letter to the FCC last month. TP-Link is ready to make “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building new, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs,” he wrote. “TP-Link is proud of this proposal and is poised to unleash this investment upon a grant of its Conditional Approval application.”

Because the Trump administration added virtually all routers to the Covered List, each router maker must obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its routers do not pose unacceptable national security risks and present a plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the US.

Router makers seeking conditional approvals must submit, among other things, details about which countries all of the components and software in its routers come from; details about parts that have only a single source and contingency plans if those suppliers become unavailable; locations of manufacturing and assembly; and a “quantitative assessment of supply chain concentration by country, expressed as both a percentage of total value and production volume.”

Router makers must also provide a “justification on why any foreign manufactured router is not currently manufactured in the United States, including why these foreign sources were selected and whether alternatives exist,” and a “detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.”

Although McIntyre would prefer that the list be focused on individual companies instead of entire product categories, she said others argue that the process benefits the US because it forces companies to think harder about where they obtain components from and to provide the government with on-shoring plans.

“I have talked to people who say, ‘Listen, you do these entire class bans, and it’s really forcing companies to really think about their supply chain… You want to have as many of these routers made in the United States as possible, just because you have a little bit more control over what’s going into the router,’” she said.

The FCC said the addition of routers was based on a determination by a White House-convened group of Executive Branch agencies with national security expertise, which said that “malicious state and non-state sponsored cyber attackers have increasingly leveraged the vulnerabilities in small and home office routers produced abroad to carry out direct attacks.” The agencies said that “routers in the United States must have trusted supply chains so we are not providing foreign actors with potential built-in backdoors to American homes, businesses, critical infrastructure, and emergency services.”

Although the FCC has generally based Covered List inclusions on determinations by other agencies, McIntyre pointed out an exception. In January 2025, the Commerce Department issued a determination about the risk of connected car hardware and software being controlled by Chinese- or Russian-controlled entities and used its own authority to prohibit transactions involving Chinese or Russian vehicle-connectivity systems.

After the Commerce determination, the FCC sought comment from the public on whether to add the vehicles to the Covered List. “That is the only example I have found of the FCC doing anything other than just taking what they were given and putting it on the Covered List,” McIntyre said.

Under the law, the FCC is required to base Covered List decisions on determinations by federal agencies with national security expertise, or the Department of Commerce. With connected cars, the FCC took public comment and has not added the vehicles to the list.

“We are not required to provide the opportunity for public input on updates to the Covered List under the Commission’s rules, and we have not done so in the past,” the FCC said in May 2025. “However, because this would be the first addition that does not include the names of specific entities, we believe that offering an opportunity for public input will help promote transparency and good governance.”

The FCC made its first Covered List addition that does not include names of specific entities seven months later, but for drones, not connected cars. The Pallone/Guthrie bill mentioned earlier in this article would limit or prevent future additions that don’t name specific entities.

“The placement on or removal from the list… of a class or category of information and communications technology or service without reference to an entity that produced or provided that technology shall be deemed a major rule” as defined in the Congressional Review Act (CRA), the bill says.

The CRA lets Congress overturn certain federal actions, including major rules. Pallone and Guthrie’s bill announcement said the Covered List process needs Congressional oversight and that their proposed “changes improve consistency and transparency around the FCC Covered List, ensuring that it targets foreign adversaries and is used as Congress intended to safeguard our national security.”

#310. Signal blocking screenshots to keep AI assistants out of private chats

A screenshot is how a lot of things get saved on a phone, from a dinner reservation to the address a friend just texted. AI assistants like Meta's Muse and Apple's Siri AI can now use what’s on the screen to answer questions or do things like add events to a calendar.

But not every platform is okay with that.

Signal, a nonprofit messaging app that uses end-to-end encryption to keep texts and calls private, is putting limits on what those assistants can see. On Friday, Nov. 20, the app announced it will block screenshots on iPhones running iOS 27 and restrict AI screen capture on some Android devices.

On iPhones running iOS 27, Signal's Block Siri AI setting is on by default. On supported Android devices, Signal automatically turns on Screen security when it detects an assistant trying to read what's on the screen. Users can turn either protection off in Signal's settings, though doing so could give an assistant with screen access a look at both sides of the conversation.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

End-to-end encryption keeps a message private on its way from one person to another. When it arrives, the recipient's phone has to turn it back into words they can read. Those words might show up in the chat itself or in a notification.

An AI assistant with access to either can read those messages, too. Once it has the text, Signal has no say in whether the assistant processes it on the phone or sends it to a remote server, according to their blog post.

Reuters worked with Signal and the AI Now Institute to see how that could happen using an Android phone and a Mac. They discovered that on the phone, Muse got the message text straight from a notification. On a Mac, it used accessibility tools and screenshots to read chats. In both tests, Muse relied on permissions granted during setup. Meta told Reuters that Muse can only access other apps through permissions users explicitly grant.

Whittaker pointed to accessibility tools, which are designed to help people with disabilities use their devices. With broad permissions, she wrote, those tools can act as "a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents."

She's thereby asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft to spell out what their assistants can read and give developers a way to block that access.

#308. Science has a home here at Ars—please help keep it that way

Your support for Ars matters more now than ever.

It’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I’ve known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It’s no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.

So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I’m unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars’ future through your support will mean I don’t have to.

But I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I’ll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

Since my start here, the central mission of Ars has been the same: cover the news in a way that helps our readers understand the facts and why they’re important. The landscape has shifted dramatically over that time—technology, science, and policy are very different from 21 years ago. But understanding those changes and why they happened matters. It matters for everything from what you should buy today to what the world you’re going to be living in 10 years from now will look like.

I’ve had the privilege of helping to decide how to translate that mission to science coverage. That decision took place against an important backdrop: While most people value things like evidence and research, they often struggle to recognize how those are used to build a body of reliable scientific information. That struggle kind of made the decision for me. Putting people in the know means helping them understand how science works as a process, and why that can produce information about the world we can trust.

Focusing on that has made our science coverage different from most of what you can get elsewhere. We don’t just tell you what’s new in the world of science; we help you understand the history of the big questions, the breakthroughs that allow us to address old problems in new ways, and the clever ideas people have for how to extract reliable information from a noisy and chaotic Universe. I’d like to think our readers get more out of that sort of writing, and it’s worth supporting.

But I’d be giving you a very incomplete picture of things if I only talked about science. Everyone at Ars has had to think about what sort of stories and presentation fit best with our mission. While our writing is essential now, it’s the people behind it that will ensure that it remains vital no matter what other changes come our way in the coming decades. And I can say with more than a little confidence that Ars is full of people you can trust to keep it that way.

One reason you can trust that is that the people at Ars now are, in many cases, the same ones who were here when you first started reading the site. We have remarkably low turnover, especially at the higher levels in our organization. There are two reasons for that: Ars is incredibly well-managed, and the people here believe in our mission.

The former is important because it should assure you that the money we get from your subscription won’t be wasted on some ill-advised pivot to video, or whatever the next craze is. The latter matters because it’s the people here who make Ars what it is. I work with some of the most thoughtful people I have ever encountered, and they all care deeply about making our work informative and compelling. I have also been lucky enough to work with a large group of freelancers over the years, and I have nothing but good things to say about them. We work hard to make sure that, even when the name on the byline is unfamiliar to you, you can be confident that you’re getting the same quality of reporting.

All of them—the full-time staff and the freelancers—are smart, great writers and know their areas of expertise better than most people in this business. Like I’m sure you do, I learn a lot from what they write (unlike you, I also get the bonus of learning from them in our Slack channels).

But it’s not just my fellow writers whom I’ve learned from. We’ve got one of the smartest communities on the Internet, with experts from pretty much every area we cover regularly contributing to the comments. In the discussions attached to my articles, I have regularly seen them fill in details I didn’t have space to mention, clarify things in response to other readers’ questions, and talk about related topics that didn’t really fit into the article. I’ve learned a lot from this, and I’m confident the rest of the readers have, too.

It’s strange to say the opposite of one of the central dogmas of the Internet: Read the comments. But it’s something I’ve told our freelance writers pretty regularly.

We’ve kept things that way even as most other sites’ comments turned toxic and were shut off. That’s taken both an editorial commitment and lots of staff time spent moderating and engaging in community management. Those don’t come for free, so your subscriptions will help support that, too.

I hope you’ll consider signing up if you’re able. Beyond the financials, I know we all appreciate it as a sign we’re on the right track.

The feature can list multiple items on e-commerce platforms for you, among other things.

Google's Gemini app for Mac now has the ability to do repetitive tasks on its own. The feature has been available to PC users for a while, but now the Mac app can also access Gemini's "Computer Use" capability. That means it can now see what's on your screen via screenshots, as well as click, type, scroll and navigate programs and websites for you. You can use the capability to automate tasks that would usually take several steps across programs and devices, as long as you tell Gemini what to do in natural language.

#304. Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings

Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.

This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.

In the new lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.

The tribe argues that every such “wager that Defendants now accept through their illegal sportsbook siphons away revenue that funds both the Tribe’s and Florida’s public programs and government services.”

Neither DraftKings nor its attorneys immediately responded to Ars’ request for comment. However, in a court filing, DraftKings says that its products available to Floridians are merely “fantasy sports and the trading of [financial] derivatives” and not gambling.

DraftKings notes that its “licensed sportsbook” operates in other states but “not in Florida.”

Multiple companies, including DraftKings, claim that their “swaps” (a type of financial derivative) are, in fact, properly governed by a federal agency, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Therefore, DraftKings argues, states cannot regulate this activity as gambling.

The Seminoles, a sovereign nation and a federally recognized tribe, have a deal with the State of Florida, known as the 2021 Gaming Compact. That 30-year contract allows the tribe to maintain what the tribe states is the “exclusive right to offer online sports betting throughout the State of Florida.” In exchange, this betting regime is regulated, and Florida takes a cut.

But since that contract was signed, attorneys for the Seminole Tribe say in the complaint, DraftKings has pursued years of court challenges and a failed ballot measure designed to break into the Sunshine State.

As of 2026, DraftKings launched “Pick6” in Florida, a game where individuals can put money down while predicting specific outcomes—for example, whether Victor Wembanyama of the San Antonio Spurs will score more or less than 28.5 points in his next basketball game.

“Based on DraftKings’ representations, Florida consumers may predictably but incorrectly conclude that Pick6 is a legal product in Florida. It is not,” the complaint states.

“Pick6 is illegal ‘gambling’ under Florida law. DraftKings operates Pick6 without a license, without state oversight, and without any consumer protections Florida requires as a condition of legal sports wagering.”

In June 2026, DraftKings launched what it calls a “Super App,” which the Seminole Tribe argues is a “one-stop shop for illegal gambling,” as it provides an interface that is “in the same format used by every traditional, regulated sportsbook.”

Florida-based professor Robert Jarvis of Nova Southeastern University studies gambling law, and he told Ars by email that he didn’t “buy the argument” DraftKings put forward that its products cannot be regulated under Florida gambling law.

Jarvis also noted that the tribe caught a break, too, with their randomly assigned federal judge.

“Not only have they had very good luck in federal court in previous cases, the federal judge assigned to the case is Ed Artau, who previously served as a Florida state trial judge (2014–20) and a Florida state appellate judge (2020–25),” he wrote. “Thus, in a sense, the Seminoles get the best of both worlds: a federal court run by a Florida state judge.”

#302. Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) review: Minor upgrades that cost too much

Meta's very best AI glasses are only slightly better than other recent models.

You'd be forgiven if you came out of Meta Connect feeling like Meta's third-generation Ray-Ban glasses seemed like a bit of an afterthought. The latest model was announced alongside the company's new audio-only glasses, its first VR glasses and an updated lineup of cheaper Meta-branded frames.

Compared with other recent glasses from the company, there's not that much new to report. Meta's latest Ray-Ban glasses have gotten some cosmetic updates and a few performance upgrades around the edges. There's still a lot to like; the frames are the most premium Meta-branded smart glasses without a display. But considering just how many variations of frames the company now makes, it's not clear that the $449 Gen 3 glasses should be your default choice if you're looking to invest in a new pair.

For now, the third-gen Meta Ray-Ban glasses only come in three frame styles: there's the classic Wayfarer frames, which have gotten a bit slimmer; Zena, a new cat-eye shape and Aviator, which Meta says is a tribute to the classic Ray-Ban design. As usual, each style is available in a number of different frame colors, many of which are semi-transparent so you can see some of the inner components if you look closely.

For this review, I wore a pair of Aviator frames in a brown tortoiseshell color called Havana. I've spent a lot of time in previous reviews complaining about glasses only coming in dark, boxy frames, so I was excited to see two new shapes. But it is disappointing that both the Zena and Aviator frames start at an eye watering $529.

Maybe it's because the new, bolder frame shapes aren't for everyone. I've owned many aviator-style sunglasses over the years, but these felt the most oversized. They are 10mm wider than the smallest Gen 3 Wayfarer frames and it definitely showed on my face. I also felt a little silly wearing thick aviator glasses with clear lenses. I understand Meta offers clear transition lenses as the default choice for most of its AI glasses because it gives people more flexibility in how they wear them. But I think this particular frame shape is better suited to sunglasses.

The bulkiness of the frames also caused some issues with the fit. The glasses constantly slipped down my nose to the point where I considered buying after-market silicon tips to keep them in place. The glasses' tips are technically adjustable, but unlike some other Meta Glasses that offer DIY adjustments, Ray-Ban Meta frames need to be adjusted professionally by an optician or at a Meta store. That's not a big deal if you buy a pair at one of these physical establishments, but it's kind of a pain if you order online.

The other major noticeable change with Gen 3 is the addition of the action button, which has appeared on other recent models of Meta glasses. It's basically a customizable shortcut that lets you trigger a specific action without a voice command. I like to set mine to "read my latest text message," but you can use it for just about any Meta AI query.

Under the hood, Gen 3 comes with two upgrades compared with Gen 2. It has a slightly better battery life, with the frames lasting "up to 9 hours" on a single charge and the charging case adding an additional 50 hours. That's about an hour better than Gen 2, but as usual, battery life can vary significantly depending on how you use them. I was able to squeeze about six hours of continuous audio playback on my pair. Features like Live AI, which uses the camera to analyze your surroundings, will drain the battery even more quickly.

Gen 3 also comes with an extra microphone, which Meta says should improve the sound quality for phone and video calls you take with your glasses. I never got any complaints with the five-mic setup on Gen 2, but people I spoke to on the phone while wearing Gen 3 assured me that I sounded clearer than I do on my AirPods Pro 2.

The latest glasses come with all the same Meta AI features as the rest of the company's lineup. The AI assistant is now powered by Muse Spark, which has generally made conversations feel more natural and reduced errors. I do miss the celebrity voices, though.

Speaking of voices, Meta has made it clear that its smart glasses will be even more important to the company as its AI agent Muse advances. The company previewed Muse on its glasses during Connect, but the feature hasn't officially rolled out yet, though a Meta support page describes it as being in "beta." Once Muse is available on the device, you'll be able to chat with your agent via your glasses and "show" it what you're seeing through the glasses' cameras. That obviously opens up a lot of interesting possibilities, though it's hard to say how big of a deal this will actually be.

I also worry that Muse and other AI features are likely to become a vehicle for Meta to more aggressively hawk Meta One subscription plans. The company has already shown a willingness to paywall some features, like its new hearing enhancement tool (which has yet to roll out). The company also seemingly considered a similar move with its other hearing-related feature Conversation Focus, which also has yet to fully roll out despite being announced more than a year ago.

And when I look at my own glasses settings, the very first menu I see is a promotion to sign up for Meta One in order to unlock more photo storage. The company is, officially, still "testing" these subscription plans, but it does raise important questions about future enshittification.

When Meta rolled out its Gen 2 Ray-Ban glasses last year, they were an obvious choice. But a lot has changed since then, and I'm not sure Gen 3 makes sense for most people. Meta's non-Ray-Ban glasses come with basically the same features for a starting price of $249. If you want the more premium finish that comes with the Ray-Ban branding, Gen 2 is still a solid option for $349, and you can still buy Gen 1 frames for $224.

So while Gen 3 can still be fairly considered "top of the line" for non-display enabled glasses, it's a much more minor distinction at this point. With all the options now available, I think the only reason to choose Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 is because you love the Ray-Ban styles (no shame in that!) or you really want that extra bit of battery life. I suspect for most people, that's not quite enough.

#301. Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone

Russia launched a Soyuz rocket with satellites to help enable drone attacks over Ukraine.

Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation’s most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX showed it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 launches on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we’ll see you again the first week of December.

Europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker. Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.

Fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE said it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements. Most of ICEYE’s satellites have launched on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets. With Falcon 9’s retirement on the horizon, ICEYE’s satellites will need rides to orbit. Avio’s Vega C rocket has a healthy backlog of contracts for European governments, but it hasn’t been a hit commercially. Investment from ICEYE could shore up Avio’s Vega rocket program and perhaps accelerate development of a new rocket.

NATO unveils launch brokerage initiative. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is contracting commercial rockets and spaceports to grow its satellite launch network and help neutralize risks to the space systems on which it relies, Bloomberg reports. NATO launched two initiatives on Tuesday: Starlift, through which participating countries can secure slots on commercial rockets, and the Global Data Marketplace, which will bolster the alliance’s military operations in space with commercial data and services.

Swimming in launches … Starlift will allow participating countries—Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey, the UK, and South Korea—to pool their military launch requirements and secure launch slots on commercial rockets. The NATO initiative will also prepare and test procedures for short-notice launches, as might be needed in a crisis. Bloomberg reported NATO’s tech agency will offer about $2.7 billion in contracts over the next two years, including to commercial space companies, AI, cyber, and command-and-control networks.

Stoke wraps up booster engine development. Stoke Space has completed development of its Zenith engine, the methane-fueled powerplant that will propel the company’s medium-class Nova rocket off the launch pad. Stoke made the announcement in a social media post Thursday. “As flight engines clear acceptance testing, we’re shipping them down to Cape Canaveral for integration with Nova’s first stage—every week,” Stoke said. Seven Zenith engines will power the Nova rocket’s reusable first stage booster, combining to generate about 700,000 pounds of thrust at full throttle.

All eyes on Stage 2 … Stoke announced it cleared a “proto-qualification” milestone on Stage 1 earlier this year. Stage 2 is undergoing cryogenic proof testing and a hot-fire test campaign at Stoke’s test complex in rural Washington. Nova’s second stage is the real innovation, with a unique arrangement of 24 thrusters surrounding a regeneratively cooled heat shield to protect it during reentry back into Earth’s atmosphere. With this, Stoke aims to fully reuse both Nova stages. The first launch is currently expected sometime next year.

Soyuz flies from Russia’s Far East. A Soyuz-2.1b rocket made its first and only launch from Russia’s Vostochny Cosmodrome this year, RussianSpaceWeb.com reports. The rocket’s Fregat upper stage deployed a new pair of high-resolution imaging satellites, along with a cluster of smaller payloads, following liftoff from Russia’s Vostochny launch base on November 14 (local time). Vostochny, located in Russia’s Far East, hosted its first space launch in 2016. By some measures, Russia spent more than $5 billion building Vostochny, only to use it for an average of two launches per year.

What was onboard? … Soyuz and Fregat carried two dual-use imaging surveillance satellites. A pair of CubeSat-class satellites for a Russian arms manufacturer were also onboard. These satellites are owned by NPO Kaisant, which specializes in drone communications and counter-drone weapons. NPO Kaisant says the satellites will join a constellation providing secure communications to Russian drones over Ukraine. A total of 12 secondary payloads were reported to be onboard, according to Roscosmos.

China’s LandSpace reports rocket reuse milestone. Three months after landing its first orbital-class rocket booster, Chinese rocket company LandSpace claims it has completed “ground acceptance and testing” of the nine methane-fueled engines recovered from the first stage of its Zhuque-3 rocket, according to Guandian News, a Chinese outlet focusing on the country’s financial and economic sector. The engines were disassembled, inspected, refurbished, reassembled, and retested after flying to space and back in August.

But wait … LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 is one of two Chinese rockets to successfully land its booster after an orbital launch attempt. The company did not say whether any of the nine engines will fly again, but don’t count on the entire Zhuque-3 booster stage from the August flight making another trip to space. The Zhuque-3 first stage toppled over soon after a seemingly flawless touchdown at LandSpace’s downrange recovery zone in northwestern China. Based on this week’s news, it appears engineers were able to salvage the engines.

SpaceX makes a historic catch. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, took a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket with the first successful catch of its enormous Starship upper stage on November 14, Ars reports. It’s hard to overstate the significance of the moment. SpaceX’s ability to recover and quickly relaunch Starships and Super Heavy boosters is central to all of the company’s lofty commercial ambitions and many of America’s high-level strategic imperatives, from national security to maintaining dominance in space exploration.

What was it like to be there? … Ars Space Editor Eric Berger covered the launch and catch of Starship from a nearby perch at Starbase, Texas. “Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower,” Berger writes. “It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks. Nevertheless, it happened.”

Vulcan fails to deliver for Amazon. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry, Ars reports. Aside from ULA itself, the fallout from the failure will strike the US military and Amazon hardest. Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is also on contract to launch roughly half of the US Space Force’s national security missions over the next few years.

Identifying the cause … ULA said Wednesday that the failure was caused by inadequate fuel supply to the first stage engines, Ars reports in a follow-up story. “ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the company said in a statement. “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.” This is fantastic news for Blue Origin, which builds the BE-4 and uses a similar design on its own New Glenn rocket. Vulcan’s solid rocket boosters also performed as expected Sunday after experiencing nozzle failures on two prior Vulcan flights.

Google taps Blue Origin for AI launch. Blue Origin announced Thursday that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that company’s Project Suncatcher program, Ars reports. Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.

Hitching a ride … Google snatched up a ride on New Glenn just as US commercial heavy-lift rockets are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has launched three times to date. The purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a company to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.

Relativity makes progress with Terran R. Another new rocket is moving closer to the launch pad. Relativity Space’s partially reusable Terran R rocket could launch sometime next year if engineers can finish development with no major setbacks. Relativity posted an update on YouTube this week, detailing several recent achievements at several of the company’s locations across the country. At Relativity headquarters in Southern California, teams have completed Terran R’s first stage thrust structure with a full set of 13 Aeon engines, fluid lines, and avionics. The engine compartment is now being integrated with Stage 1 tankage. Terran R’s second stage recently completed its first all-up test firing at Stennis Space Center, Mississippi.

Meanwhile, at Cape Canaveral … Relativity is also moving forward with the Terran R launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The launch pad’s lightning protection towers are now complete, as is the steel framing for Terran R’s launch table. Work continues on the rocket’s transporter-erector, strongback, and the launch pad’s propellant storage tanks.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#300. You can reveal the full GTA 6 map in minutes using this simple plane trick

Clear up that fog in no time at all, but be careful.

GTA 6 has a huge map, which is around twice as big as the one found with GTA 5. That's a whole lot of Florida-inspired strip malls and alligator-soaked swamps. However, new players start the game in a fairly remote region, based on the Florida Keys, and the vast majority of the map is unavailable for perusal.

Fog is obscuring every part of the map that you haven't explored yet. New regions get uncovered as you travel through them. You could do this the long way, by following the story. You could also do this the slightly-shorter way, by grabbing a car and just driving north until the wheels fall off. GTA 6 doesn't have a system in place that automatically ups the wanted level as you enter new areas, so that's good.

However, the quickest way to unlock the full map is found in the skies, and not the roads. Long-time players know the drill. Jason needs to get an airplane.

Luckily, there's a plane just a few miles north of Jason's first house in Key Lento. Take a break from making home renovations and head to Southpoint Airfield, as seen in the map above. It's basically just north of the starting area.

Drive the western bridge that runs over the Shoeless Keys and then head west a little bit onto a runway. It's hard to miss. The area is marked as restricted, but it's mostly abandoned so there shouldn't be any armed onlookers.

Once at the airfield, look for a duster plane just waiting to be flown. Hop in and do your thing. Planes move incredibly fast and will quickly unlock all of those foggy areas. Just fly carefully and keep an eye on fuel.

You probably won't be able to get the whole map done on a single fly through, due to that fuel, but planes automatically regenerate at airfields as soon as one leaves. Fly back to Southpoint and start again, this time heading in another direction. You'll have the whole map uncovered in minutes.

Happy travels. The only real thing to worry about here is the Mile Zero Air Station at the bottom left of the map. Flying over that airspace will instantly generate a four-star wanted rating. This wanted level can bring police after you in helicopters, so airplanes aren't necessarily safe. Save this area for last and exit as soon as the fog lifts from the map. Mile Zero is home to some really fast aircraft, but it's likely not worth the trouble just yet.

#298. FIFA presidential election 2027: Infantino facing Diallo and Tashima — could an alliance change everything?

Two challengers to Gianni Infantino have registered for next year's FIFA presidential election. What do Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima stand for – and do they stand a chance against the incumbent?

Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 member nations of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.

Gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under Infantino's leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.

During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia — a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.

At the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.

Infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate — whether exemplified by his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly after the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.

A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has also placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment plan, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.

Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.

He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).

"Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement announcing the German FA's position.

"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction."

Diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.

The third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.

During a press conference in the Japanese capital Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.

"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he said.

"Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization."

Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations — the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino — makes him a longshot to win the election.

But he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.

"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," he said.

"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.

However, Tashima also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.

If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

#297. Chelsea searches for new manager as Premier League breaks record for most sackings in a single season

It was just six months ago that Graham Potter was deemed the man to usher in a fresh, exciting era at Chelsea.

The club’s new ownership group, led by American businessman Todd Boehly, had enticed Potter away from Brighton with the promise of managing one of the most lucrative teams in world soccer.

More than $600 million was spent on bringing big-name players to the club and Potter, one of the most exciting young managers in the Premier League, was to mold them into a winning machine.

Chelsea has spent over $600 million on new signings. Here's why that's significant

But, on Sunday, the club announced that it had sacked its manager after an underwhelming spell in charge.

Potter managed to win just 10 of the 28 league matches this season and leaves the team 11th in the Premier League table.

In recent weeks, players had looked a shadow of their former selves and many fans had lost confidence that Potter’s plan for the club could ever work.

Eventually, after previously sticking by its manager, Blues ownership agreed.

“On behalf of everyone at the club, we want to thank Graham sincerely for his contribution to Chelsea,” the club’s co-owners Todd Boehly and Behdad Eghbali said in a statement.

“We have the highest degree of respect for Graham as a coach and as a person. He has always conducted himself with professionalism and integrity and we are all disappointed in this outcome.”

In his previous role as Brighton manager, Potter was given time to stamp his identity on the squad.

The club was punching above its weight financially and, as a result, carefully selected new signings which would compliment Potter’s style of play.

The approach paid off as the team became an established Premier League outfit which has gone on to greater things this season – the Seagulls currently sit sixth in the league and in the UEFA Conference League qualification spot.

At Chelsea, it seemed the complete opposite.

As was the case under previous owner Roman Abramovich, the club expected instant results and used its financial weight to sign a number of high-profile names, including the likes of Enzo Fernández and Mykhailo Mudryk.

Despite his impressive CV, Potter had never managed superstars and suddenly found himself in a changing room with multiple.

The scatter gun approach to recruitment also left the team lacking balance and organization with Potter failing to get a tune out of a team busting with talent.

In truth, many had raised an eyebrow when Potter, inexperienced at the very top level, was chosen to replace Thomas Tuchel as manager.

Despite falling out of favor with fans by the end of his tenure, Tuchel had guided Chelsea to the Champions League title in 2021 and is still considered by many as one of the best coaches in the world.

The German has gone on to sign with Bavarian giant Bayern Munich through the 2024/25 season and recently told reporters he needed “quite a bit of time to distance himself from Chelsea” because leaving the club had hurt him.

Bayern Munich sacks manager Julian Nagelsmann, appoints Thomas Tuchel

“Todd [Boehly] said he would be different to Roman [Abramovich],” former Liverpool player and current pundit Jamie Carragher wrote on Twitter.

“I feel for Graham Potter, but it was inevitable. You don’t change Tuchel for Potter. Ridiculous decision to start with.”

With 10 games left in the league and a Champions League quarterfinal against Real Madrid on the horizon, Chelsea still has plenty to play for.

Assistant coach Bruno Saltor will take over on an interim basis, but Boehly and his team must now look for a long-term replacement capable – and willing – to bring order to Chelsea’s chaos.

Potter’s sacking is yet another sign of just how transient managers can be in the top-flight of English football, especially when results aren’t instantaneous.

There has now been a record 12 sackings in the Premier League so far this season, with Potter leaving his position the same day Leicester boss Brendan Rodgers was sacked from his.

The previous record was 10 manager changes in a single season, set in four other campaigns, most recently in 2017/18.

#294. SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space

Bondholders want SpaceX’s valuable chip collateral kept on Earth and within reach.

Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.

The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.

SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.

It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.

The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.

The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.

SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.

The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people said. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.

The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.

More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.

Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.

SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.

Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.

The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.

“The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” said Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.

“This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he said.

Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in New York.

#292. Some fans whistle as Lionel Messi's name is announced as Paris Saint-Germain's season hits new low

Paris Saint-Germain’s miserable season went from bad to worse on Sunday as the team suffered a second straight home defeat with a 1-0 loss to Lyon.

Even before the game kicked off, Lionel Messi bore the brunt of the frustrations of some PSG fans who whistled when his name appeared on the big screen during the announcement of the starting lineup.

Lionel Messi passes 100 international goals with hat-trick against Curaçao

After Alexadre Lacazette missed a first-half penalty, Bradley Barcola’s goal 10 minutes into the second period was enough to earn Lyon the three points on a night that PSG rarely looked like threatening the visiting goal.

Lens’ 1-0 victory over Rennes and Marseille’s 1-1 draw with Montepellier means both teams are now just six points behind PSG at the top of Ligue 1, and even the domestic title may slip from the team’s grasp.

The reaction of some fans on Sunday must have felt a world away from the adulation and worship Messi received during his recent return to Argentina for friendlies against Panama and Curaçao as the country continued its World Cup celebrations.

Messi’s arrival at the Parc des Princes was supposed to be the missing piece that would help PSG finally win the Champions League, the trophy the club’s Qatari owners crave the most.

So far, the only major trophy the team has won since Messi joined was Ligue 1 last season, a title – it’s fair to say – PSG would likely have won without him.

Messi has 34 goal contributions in all competitions for PSG this season – 18 goals and 17 assists – second only to Mbappé’s 38 and head coach Christophe Galtier refused to lay the blame for the team’s failures at the Argentine’s feet.

“I found it [the jeering] hard to listen to,” Galtier told reporters, per the Athletic. “There may be expectations for Messi and Mbappe to unlock difficult situations. Messi tries very hard, they didn’t all work out; but around him, the other players also need to do their jobs.”

“We can’t expect everything from Leo and Kylian,” he added.

Lionel Messi mania grips Argentina as World Cup celebrations continue

Up next for PSG is a season-defining week as Galtier’s side travels to a Nice team that is unbeaten in 13 matches, before hosting Lens at the Parc des Princes.

PSG has lost two of its three matches since being dumped out of the Champions League by Bayern Munich last month, and only limped past relegation-threatened Brest with a 90th minute Kylian Mbappé winner.

After his team’s victory, Lyon head coach Laurent Blanc said the Champions League or bust mentality has been detrimental to PSG’s performances.

“Paris’ problem is when the No. 1 objective of the Champions League is no longer accessible, it seems that the season no longer exists – and at all levels,” he told reporters.

#291. Here's everything GTA+ gets you in GTA 6: Is it worth $8 a month?

GTA+ adds a few perks to GTA 6 and one of them is already stirring up players.

A lot has changed in gaming in the 13 years since Grand Theft Auto 5 debuted. That includes the explosion of live-service games and gaming subscriptions, and the Grand Theft Auto franchise has gotten in on both with GTA Online and the GTA+ membership. Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is out, GTA+ members get some additional benefits in the new game on top of what the subscription already offers in GTA Online.

If you're new to GTA+, you can sign up for it in-game or through your console's digital storefront. Digital pre-orders of GTA 6 on PlayStation and Xbox also included a free month of GTA+ to try it out. If you didn't pre-order or you want to keep the subscription after the free month ends, it costs $8 a month.

That $8 gets you a few perks in GTA 6, but nothing game-changing. You'll get 10 percent more money for any eligible vehicles you sell in the game and a 10 percent discount at a variety of stores. You can also use in-game transport options like scooters, bikes and public transit for free and get a premium membership to the RydeMe rideshare service. Together, those perks add up to a few cheaper ways to get around GTA 6's huge map and an easier time making cash. That can make a big difference in your progress early in the game, since cheats don't unlock until you beat the story.

The biggest and most controversial benefit is one you can claim only after reaching GTA 6's third chapter. At that point, you'll get the '90 Annis Venturas BLVD Elegy, a free sports car, plus a garage in the Crosstown area. Locking exclusive items in a single-player game behind a monthly subscription is never popular, and players have already voiced their displeasure on Reddit.

For most players, the GTA+ subscription fee probably isn't worth it for what it adds to GTA 6 alone. From the start, GTA+ has focused mostly on GTA Online, giving members in-game currency and discounts, new vehicles and garages to store them in, and a rotating suite of items and features. For dedicated GTA Online players who also picked up GTA 6, there's a much better case for the subscription.

The game library included with GTA+ might make it worth it for more people. Anyone with an active subscription also gets access to a selection of Rockstar's other games, including Red Dead Redemption and GTA 5. Of course, you might not have time for any of those until you finish a campaign that can run 80 hours, but the library does make the $8 subscription much easier to justify.
